paragraph.text: I34. "Carmine is a natural dye, better than artificial ones"

carmine, or cochineal dye, is made from insects: female cochineals, which live on cacti, are dropped into hot water, dried and ground, and about 70,000 are needed to make a pound of dye. Being natural says nothing about who was killed to make it. And there are natural red dyes from plants, such as those from beetroot, paprika, tomato and purple fruits. Carmine shows up in yogurts, drinks, sweets, processed meats, lipsticks and eyeshadows, sometimes under unclear names such as E120 or CI 75470.

Some yogurts, candies and lipsticks are red because of a dye made from little bugs called cochineals. To make a little dye, thousands of them are killed. You can make things red with beetroot, strawberry or paprika, without hurting any creature.

Carmine is made from cochineals: about 70,000 females, killed in hot water, are needed for a pound of dye. Being natural doesn't change that. And the choice isn't between carmine and artificial dye: there are natural reds from beetroot, paprika, tomato and purple fruits. If you want to avoid it, look on the label for "carmine", "cochineal", "E120", "INS 120" or, in cosmetics, "CI 75470".

text.bold: 3. Insect sentience is a serious possibility.

paragraph.text: The 2024 New York Declaration on Animal Consciousness recognizes a realistic possibility of consciousness in insects. Cochineals have been little studied, and doubt, in the face of such large numbers, is a reason for caution.
Beetroot, anthocyanins, paprika and lycopene give red and pink tones without killing animals. The comparison with artificial dyes is a false choice.
Since 2011, the US Food and Drug Administration has required carmine to be declared by name on food and cosmetic labels, because of reports of severe allergic reactions.

It's true that some artificial red dyes raise health concerns, that carmine is natural and has been used for centuries, and that it is stable.
But it costs the lives of thousands of insects per pound, and there are natural plant reds. Natural and victim-free aren't the same thing.
